contents.text: Experiences from early in someone's life can shape his or her actions later in life. So, historians often consider a person's background when studying historical figures. Read about Jackson's life and career before becoming president. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: Andrew Jackson is born near the present-day border of North and South Carolina. At age 14, he fights on the Patriot side against Great Britain during the Revolutionary War.

After studying law, Jackson moves to Nashville, a western frontier town in what becomes Tennessee. He eventually gains enough wealth to own a large farm called a plantation, purchase enslaved people, and buy and sell land.
Jackson is elected as the first U.S. representative from the new state of Tennessee. He later serves as a state judge and as a commander of the state militia.
Jackson leads military forces to victory against Creek Native Americans in the Mississippi Territory, resulting in the forced transfer of 23 million acres of Creek land to the United States.
Jackson gains national fame by leading U.S. forces to victory against Britain in the Battle of New Orleans at the end of the War of 1812.
Jackson leads U.S. forces to victory against Seminole Native Americans in Florida, which allows the United States to buy Florida from Spain in 1819.

contents.text: After the War of 1812, many Americans felt a sense of national pride and unity. One Boston newspaper called this period the "Era of Good Feelings." Americans spread westward, the economy improved, and one party—the Democratic-Republicans—dominated national politics. But significant divisions emerged in the mid-1820s, especially during the contentious presidential election of 1824. Read about the election and its outcome. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: In 1824, four Democratic-Republican candidates ran for president: John Quincy Adams, Henry Clay, William Crawford, and Andrew Jackson. Jackson received the most popular and Electoral College votes, but he didn't win
50 percent of the electoral vote, which the Constitution requires to win the presidency. In this scenario, the Constitution requires the House of Representatives to decide the election's outcome.

textContent.text: Henry Clay, as the fourth-place candidate, was immediately removed from consideration. However, Clay distrusted Jackson and used his role as Speaker of the House to convince his supporters to elect Adams. President Adams then chose Clay as his secretary of state, an important cabinet position that was seen as a path to the presidency. Jackson condemned the arrangement as a "corrupt bargain" that ignored the will of the voters. He and his allies spent the next four years vocally opposing the Adams administration, accusing it of corruption and ignoring common people's needs. These tensions created a long-term split in the Democratic-Republican Party between Adams supporters and Jackson supporters.

contents.text: After losing the 1824 presidential election, Andrew Jackson immediately began campaigning for the 1828 election. He employed Martin Van Buren, a New York politician, to run his campaign. Under Van Buren's leadership, Jackson's faction, meaning group, of Democratic-Republicans made several changes to political organizing that were adopted by other political parties. This faction became known as the Democratic Party, considered by historians to be the first modern political party.
Match each Democratic Party innovation to the earlier political practice it changed.

draggableItems.text: Democrats used public meetings to select candidates, giving more people a voice in choosing their representatives.
Democrats developed a highly organized party system called a political machine, which enforced party unity and rewarded allies with political offices.
Democrats criticized the old system as undemocratic and urged people from a wider range of social classes to enter politics.
Democrats favored patronage, meaning newly elected presidents replaced most government officials with party allies.

staticItems.text: The nation was dominated by social elites, such as wealthy landowners, plantation owners, merchants, and bankers.
Many government roles were filled by career officials who remained in their positions across multiple presidential administrations.
Political parties were disorganized and ineffective since leaders were reluctant to support them.
Political candidates were chosen by a small group of party insiders.

contents.text: After the War of 1812, many Americans felt a sense of national pride and unity. One Boston newspaper called this period the "Era of Good Feelings." Americans spread westward, the economy improved, and one party—the Democratic-Republicans—dominated national politics. But significant divisions emerged in the mid-1820s, especially during the contentious presidential election of 1824. Read about the election and its outcome. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: In 1824, four Democratic-Republican candidates ran for president: John Quincy Adams, Henry Clay, William Crawford, and Andrew Jackson. Jackson received the most popular and Electoral College votes, but he didn't win
50 percent of the electoral vote, which the Constitution requires to win the presidency. In this scenario, the Constitution requires the House of Representatives to decide the election's outcome.

textContent.text: Henry Clay, as the fourth-place candidate, was immediately removed from consideration. However, Clay distrusted Jackson and used his role as Speaker of the House to convince his supporters to elect Adams. President Adams then chose Clay as his secretary of state, an important cabinet position that was seen as a path to the presidency. Jackson condemned the arrangement as a "corrupt bargain" that ignored the will of the voters. He and his allies spent the next four years vocally opposing the Adams administration, accusing it of corruption and ignoring common people's needs. These tensions created a long-term split in the Democratic-Republican Party between Adams supporters and Jackson supporters.

contents.text: After losing the 1824 presidential election, Andrew Jackson immediately began campaigning for the 1828 election. He employed Martin Van Buren, a New York politician, to run his campaign. Under Van Buren's leadership, Jackson's faction, meaning group, of Democratic-Republicans made several changes to political organizing that were adopted by other political parties. This faction became known as the Democratic Party, considered by historians to be the first modern political party.

contents.text: After the War of 1812, many Americans felt a sense of national pride and unity. One Boston newspaper called this period the "Era of Good Feelings." Americans spread westward, the economy improved, and one party—the Democratic-Republicans—dominated national politics. But significant divisions emerged in the mid-1820s, especially during the contentious presidential election of 1824. Read about the election and its outcome. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: In 1824, four Democratic-Republican candidates ran for president: John Quincy Adams, Henry Clay, William Crawford, and Andrew Jackson. Jackson received the most popular and Electoral College votes, but he didn't win
50 percent of the electoral vote, which the Constitution requires to win the presidency. In this scenario, the Constitution requires the House of Representatives to decide the election's outcome.

textContent.text: Henry Clay, as the fourth-place candidate, was immediately removed from consideration. However, Clay distrusted Jackson and used his role as Speaker of the House to convince his supporters to elect Adams. President Adams then chose Clay as his secretary of state, an important cabinet position that was seen as a path to the presidency. Jackson condemned the arrangement as a "corrupt bargain" that ignored the will of the voters. He and his allies spent the next four years vocally opposing the Adams administration, accusing it of corruption and ignoring common people's needs. These tensions created a long-term split in the Democratic-Republican Party between Adams supporters and Jackson supporters.

contents.text: After losing the 1824 presidential election, Andrew Jackson immediately began campaigning for the 1828 election. He employed Martin Van Buren, a New York politician, to run his campaign. Under Van Buren's leadership, Jackson's faction, meaning group, of Democratic-Republicans made several changes to political organizing that were adopted by other political parties. This faction became known as the Democratic Party, considered by historians to be the first modern political party.
Match each Democratic Party innovation to the earlier political practice it changed.

draggableItems.text: Democrats favored patronage, meaning newly elected presidents replaced most government officials with party allies.
Democrats developed a highly organized party system called a political machine, which enforced party unity and rewarded allies with political offices.
Democrats criticized the old system as undemocratic and urged people from a wider range of social classes to enter politics.
Democrats used public meetings to select candidates, giving more people a voice in choosing their representatives.

The nation was dominated by social elites, such as wealthy landowners, plantation owners, merchants, and bankers.
Political parties were disorganized and ineffective since leaders were reluctant to support them.

contents.text: After the War of 1812, many Americans felt a sense of national pride and unity. One Boston newspaper called this period the "Era of Good Feelings." Americans spread westward, the economy improved, and one party—the Democratic-Republicans—dominated national politics. But significant divisions emerged in the mid-1820s, especially during the contentious presidential election of 1824. Read about the election and its outcome. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: In 1824, four Democratic-Republican candidates ran for president: John Quincy Adams, Henry Clay, William Crawford, and Andrew Jackson. Jackson received the most popular and Electoral College votes, but he didn't win
50 percent of the electoral vote, which the Constitution requires to win the presidency. In this scenario, the Constitution requires the House of Representatives to decide the election's outcome.

textContent.text: Henry Clay, as the fourth-place candidate, was immediately removed from consideration. However, Clay distrusted Jackson and used his role as Speaker of the House to convince his supporters to elect Adams. President Adams then chose Clay as his secretary of state, an important cabinet position that was seen as a path to the presidency. Jackson condemned the arrangement as a "corrupt bargain" that ignored the will of the voters. He and his allies spent the next four years vocally opposing the Adams administration, accusing it of corruption and ignoring common people's needs. These tensions created a long-term split in the Democratic-Republican Party between Adams supporters and Jackson supporters.

contents.text: Under the United States Constitution, Native American communities are treated as separate governments, similar to foreign nations. As the country grew westward after the American Revolution, the U.S. government signed a series of treaties with Native American groups. Read the excerpts from three of these treaties. Then follow the instructions below.

content.text: <citation>This treaty was signed by the United States government and the Cherokee people in Georgia.</citation>

If any citizen of the United States, or other person not being an Indian, shall attempt to settle on any of the lands westward or southward of the said boundary which are hereby allotted to the Indians for their hunting grounds…the Indians may punish him or not as they please…Congress…shall have the sole and exclusive right of regulating the trade with the Indians…
<citation>This treaty was signed by the United States government and the Cherokee people in Georgia.</citation>

It is agreed on the part of the Cherokees, that the United States shall have the sole and exclusive right of regulating their trade.…The United States solemnly guarantee to the Cherokee Nation, all their lands not hereby [given to the U.S. government].…If any citizen of the United States, or other person not being an Indian, shall settle on any of the Cherokees' lands, such person shall forfeit the protection of the United States, and the Cherokees may punish him or not, as they please.
<citation>This treaty was signed by the United States government and several Native American communities in present-day Ohio.</citation>

[When] those tribes [want] to sell their lands, or any part of them, they are to be sold only to the United States.…And the said Indian tribes again acknowledge themselves to be under the protection of the said United States, and no other power whatever.…If any citizen of the United States, or any other white person or persons, shall presume to settle upon the lands now relinquished by the United States, such citizen or other person shall be out of the protection of the United States; and the Indian tribe, on whose land the settlement shall be made, may drive off the settler, or punish him in such manner as they shall think fit…

contents.text: In the late 1700s and early 1800s, United States officials adopted a policy of "civilization," which pushed Native American groups to adopt many white American practices. Read the passage about the United States's "civilization" policy. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Many white Americans argued that Native American communities must abandon traditional farming and hunting practices in order to survive. So they pushed "civilization" policies to force Native American people to adopt white American culture. In 1819, for example, Congress paid Christian missionaries to establish schools in Native American territories. These schools taught reading, writing, and math, while also trying to convince people to convert to Christianity.

Another part of "civilization" policy targeted land ownership. In most Native American tribes, land belonged to the entire community. But U.S. policymakers wanted to distribute communal land so it was owned by individual Native Americans. They hoped this would make it easier for white Americans to purchase more land.

Many Native American communities resisted "civilization" policy by refusing to give up communal land ownership and maintaining their traditional economic, social, and religious practices. Other communities only adopted aspects of white American culture that could benefit them. For example, men hunted with guns instead of bows and arrows, and women made clothing from European cloth instead of deerskin. Additionally, some Native American people adopted Christianity and learned to speak and write English.

contents.text: Which of the following accurately describes how Native Americans responded to the United States's "civilization" policy?

choices.text: Native American people adopted some economic and social practices of white Americans but resisted attempts to break up their land.
Native American communities rejected all white American practices and instead revived traditional farming and hunting practices.
Christian missionaries who moved to Native American land failed to convert any Native American people there.
Many white Americans who attempted to "civilize" Native American groups instead adopted Native American farming and hunting practices.

contents.text: One central conflict between white Americans and Native Americans involved the Cherokee people, who lived in present-day Georgia, Alabama, Tennessee, and North Carolina. Those states, especially Georgia, challenged the right of the Cherokees to live within their state boundaries. In order to strengthen their position as an independent government, Cherokee leaders wrote and adopted a constitution in 1827 that was modeled after that of the United States.

contents.text: In a series of decisions in the 1820s and 1830s, the Supreme Court clarified the role of the federal and state governments in dealing with Native American groups:

elements.text: In 1823, the Supreme Court decided that Native American individuals could only sell their land to the United States government, not to an individual or a U.S. state.
In 1831, the Supreme Court ruled that the Cherokees were a "domestic dependent nation" with a right to exist within Georgia's boundaries.
In 1832, the Supreme Court ruled that Georgia could not pass laws regulating Cherokee people. Instead, only the federal government could make legal agreements with Native American tribes.

contents.text: Under the United States Constitution, Native American communities are treated as separate governments, similar to foreign nations. As the country grew westward after the American Revolution, the U.S. government signed a series of treaties with Native American groups. Read the excerpts from three of these treaties. Then answer the question below.

content.text: <citation>This treaty was signed by the United States government and the Cherokee people in Georgia.</citation>

If any citizen of the United States, or other person not being an Indian, shall attempt to settle on any of the lands westward or southward of the said boundary which are hereby allotted to the Indians for their hunting grounds…the Indians may punish him or not as they please…Congress…shall have the sole and exclusive right of regulating the trade with the Indians…
<citation>This treaty was signed by the United States government and the Cherokee people in Georgia.</citation>

It is agreed on the part of the Cherokees, that the United States shall have the sole and exclusive right of regulating their trade.…The United States solemnly guarantee to the Cherokee Nation, all their lands not hereby [given to the U.S. government].…If any citizen of the United States, or other person not being an Indian, shall settle on any of the Cherokees' lands, such person shall forfeit the protection of the United States, and the Cherokees may punish him or not, as they please.
<citation>This treaty was signed by the United States government and several Native American communities in present-day Ohio.</citation>

[When] those tribes [want] to sell their lands, or any part of them, they are to be sold only to the United States.…And the said Indian tribes again acknowledge themselves to be under the protection of the said United States, and no other power whatever.…If any citizen of the United States, or any other white person or persons, shall presume to settle upon the lands now relinquished by the United States, such citizen or other person shall be out of the protection of the United States; and the Indian tribe, on whose land the settlement shall be made, may drive off the settler, or punish him in such manner as they shall think fit…

contents.text: In the late 1700s and early 1800s, United States officials adopted a policy of "civilization," which pushed Native American groups to adopt many white American practices. Read the passage about the United States's "civilization" policy. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: Many white Americans argued that Native American communities must abandon traditional farming and hunting practices in order to survive. So they pushed "civilization" policies to force Native American people to adopt white American culture. In 1819, for example, Congress paid Christian missionaries to establish schools in Native American territories. These schools taught reading, writing, and math, while also trying to convince people to convert to Christianity.

Another part of "civilization" policy targeted land ownership. In most Native American tribes, land belonged to the entire community. But U.S. policymakers wanted to distribute communal land so it was owned by individual Native Americans. They hoped this would make it easier for white Americans to purchase more land.

Many Native American communities resisted "civilization" policy by refusing to give up communal land ownership and maintaining their traditional economic, social, and religious practices. Other communities only adopted aspects of white American culture that could benefit them. For example, men hunted with guns instead of bows and arrows, and women made clothing from European cloth instead of deerskin. Additionally, some Native American people adopted Christianity and learned to speak and write English.

contents.text: One central conflict between white Americans and Native Americans involved the Cherokee people, who lived in present-day Georgia, Alabama, Tennessee, and North Carolina. contents.text: In a series of decisions in the 1820s and 1830s, the Supreme Court clarified the role of the federal and state governments in dealing with Native American groups:

elements.text: In 1823, the Supreme Court decided that Native American individuals could only sell their land to the United States government, not to an individual or a U.S. state.
In 1831, the Supreme Court ruled that the Cherokees were a "domestic dependent nation" with a right to exist within Georgia's boundaries.
In 1832, the Supreme Court ruled that Georgia could not pass laws regulating Cherokee people. Instead, only the federal government could make legal agreements with Native American tribes.

contents.text: The last two rulings seemed like victories for the Cherokee Nation, but they relied on the federal government to enforce decisions. President Andrew Jackson did not believe Native American nations should exist within U.S. states, so he allowed Georgia to continue its efforts to drive out Cherokee people.

contents.text: Under the United States Constitution, Native American communities are treated as separate governments, similar to foreign nations. As the country grew westward after the American Revolution, the U.S. government signed a series of treaties with Native American groups. Read the excerpts from three of these treaties. Then follow the instructions below.

content.text: <citation>This treaty was signed by the United States government and the Cherokee people in Georgia.</citation>

If any citizen of the United States, or other person not being an Indian, shall attempt to settle on any of the lands westward or southward of the said boundary which are hereby allotted to the Indians for their hunting grounds…the Indians may punish him or not as they please…Congress…shall have the sole and exclusive right of regulating the trade with the Indians…
<citation>This treaty was signed by the United States government and the Cherokee people in Georgia.</citation>

It is agreed on the part of the Cherokees, that the United States shall have the sole and exclusive right of regulating their trade.…The United States solemnly guarantee to the Cherokee Nation, all their lands not hereby [given to the U.S. government].…If any citizen of the United States, or other person not being an Indian, shall settle on any of the Cherokees' lands, such person shall forfeit the protection of the United States, and the Cherokees may punish him or not, as they please.
<citation>This treaty was signed by the United States government and several Native American communities in present-day Ohio.</citation>

[When] those tribes [want] to sell their lands, or any part of them, they are to be sold only to the United States.…And the said Indian tribes again acknowledge themselves to be under the protection of the said United States, and no other power whatever.…If any citizen of the United States, or any other white person or persons, shall presume to settle upon the lands now relinquished by the United States, such citizen or other person shall be out of the protection of the United States; and the Indian tribe, on whose land the settlement shall be made, may drive off the settler, or punish him in such manner as they shall think fit…

contents.text: In the late 1700s and early 1800s, United States officials adopted a policy of "civilization," which pushed Native American groups to adopt many white American practices. Read the passage about the United States's "civilization" policy. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Many white Americans argued that Native American communities must abandon traditional farming and hunting practices in order to survive. So they pushed "civilization" policies to force Native American people to adopt white American culture. In 1819, for example, Congress paid Christian missionaries to establish schools in Native American territories. These schools taught reading, writing, and math, while also trying to convince people to convert to Christianity.

Another part of "civilization" policy targeted land ownership. In most Native American tribes, land belonged to the entire community. But U.S. policymakers wanted to distribute communal land so it was owned by individual Native Americans. They hoped this would make it easier for white Americans to purchase more land.

Many Native American communities resisted "civilization" policy by refusing to give up communal land ownership and maintaining their traditional economic, social, and religious practices. Other communities only adopted aspects of white American culture that could benefit them. For example, men hunted with guns instead of bows and arrows, and women made clothing from European cloth instead of deerskin. Additionally, some Native American people adopted Christianity and learned to speak and write English.

contents.text: One central conflict between white Americans and Native Americans involved the Cherokee people, who lived in present-day Georgia, Alabama, Tennessee, and North Carolina. Those states, especially Georgia, challenged the right of the Cherokees to live within their state boundaries. In order to strengthen their position as an independent government, Cherokee leaders wrote and adopted a constitution in 1827 that was modeled after that of the United States.
Match each modified excerpt from the Cherokee Constitution with its meaning.

draggableItems.text: The Cherokee territory borders have been guaranteed by treaties with the U.S. and cannot be reduced.
If a Cherokee person moves outside of Cherokee territory and becomes a U.S. citizen, that person can no longer be a Cherokee citizen.
The Cherokee government will have three branches—a legislature, a Principal Chief, and a Supreme Court—similar to the U.S. government.
Cherokee land is owned by all Cherokee people, but anything built on that land is owned by the individual who built it.
Cherokee people may not sell their land to the United States, a U.S. state, or a U.S. citizen.

staticItems.text: The boundaries of this Nation, embracing the lands solemnly guaranteed and reserved forever to the Cherokee Nation by the Treaties concluded with the United States…shall forever hereafter remain unalterably the same…

The Sovereignty and Jurisdiction of this Government shall extend over the country within the boundaries above described, and the lands therein… shall remain the common property of the Nation; but the improvements made thereon, and in the possession of the citizens of the Nation, are the exclusive… property of the citizens…
[The] citizens of the Nation…shall possess no right nor power to dispose of their property in any manner whatever to the United States, individual states, nor to individual citizens hereof…

[Whenever] any such citizen or citizens shall remove with their effects out of the limits of this Nation, and become citizens of any other government, all their rights and privileges as citizens of this Nation shall cease…

contents.text: In a series of decisions in the 1820s and 1830s, the Supreme Court clarified the role of the federal and state governments in dealing with Native American groups:

elements.text: In 1823, the Supreme Court decided that Native American individuals could only sell their land to the United States government, not to an individual or a U.S. state.
In 1831, the Supreme Court ruled that the Cherokees were a "domestic dependent nation" with a right to exist within Georgia's boundaries.
In 1832, the Supreme Court ruled that Georgia could not pass laws regulating Cherokee people. Instead, only the federal government could make legal agreements with Native American tribes.

contents.text: The last two rulings seemed like victories for the Cherokee Nation, but they relied on the federal government to enforce decisions. contents.text: Under the United States Constitution, Native American communities are treated as separate governments, similar to foreign nations. As the country grew westward after the American Revolution, the U.S. government signed a series of treaties with Native American groups. Read the excerpts from three of these treaties. Then answer the question below.

content.text: <citation>This treaty was signed by the United States government and the Cherokee people in Georgia.</citation>

If any citizen of the United States, or other person not being an Indian, shall attempt to settle on any of the lands westward or southward of the said boundary which are hereby allotted to the Indians for their hunting grounds…the Indians may punish him or not as they please…Congress…shall have the sole and exclusive right of regulating the trade with the Indians…
<citation>This treaty was signed by the United States government and the Cherokee people in Georgia.</citation>

It is agreed on the part of the Cherokees, that the United States shall have the sole and exclusive right of regulating their trade.…The United States solemnly guarantee to the Cherokee Nation, all their lands not hereby [given to the U.S. government].…If any citizen of the United States, or other person not being an Indian, shall settle on any of the Cherokees' lands, such person shall forfeit the protection of the United States, and the Cherokees may punish him or not, as they please.
<citation>This treaty was signed by the United States government and several Native American communities in present-day Ohio.</citation>

[When] those tribes [want] to sell their lands, or any part of them, they are to be sold only to the United States.…And the said Indian tribes again acknowledge themselves to be under the protection of the said United States, and no other power whatever.…If any citizen of the United States, or any other white person or persons, shall presume to settle upon the lands now relinquished by the United States, such citizen or other person shall be out of the protection of the United States; and the Indian tribe, on whose land the settlement shall be made, may drive off the settler, or punish him in such manner as they shall think fit…

contents.text: In the late 1700s and early 1800s, United States officials adopted a policy of "civilization," which pushed Native American groups to adopt many white American practices. Read the passage about the United States's "civilization" policy. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: Many white Americans argued that Native American communities must abandon traditional farming and hunting practices in order to survive. So they pushed "civilization" policies to force Native American people to adopt white American culture. In 1819, for example, Congress paid Christian missionaries to establish schools in Native American territories. These schools taught reading, writing, and math, while also trying to convince people to convert to Christianity.

Another part of "civilization" policy targeted land ownership. In most Native American tribes, land belonged to the entire community. But U.S. policymakers wanted to distribute communal land so it was owned by individual Native Americans. They hoped this would make it easier for white Americans to purchase more land.

Many Native American communities resisted "civilization" policy by refusing to give up communal land ownership and maintaining their traditional economic, social, and religious practices. Other communities only adopted aspects of white American culture that could benefit them. For example, men hunted with guns instead of bows and arrows, and women made clothing from European cloth instead of deerskin. Additionally, some Native American people adopted Christianity and learned to speak and write English.

period. Antebellum means "before the war," referring to the time period before the Civil War (1861–1865). In the antebellum period, many Americans worried about the social problems they saw around them. To help solve these problems, some people started
, or efforts to improve society.

contents.text: Match each social problem with the reform movement that tried to solve it.

draggableItems.text: The abolition movement worked to end slavery in the United States.
The prison reform movement built penitentiaries where prisoners could receive counseling and education.
The moral treatment movement stressed the need for specialized mental hospitals.

contents.text: Look back at the passage. These choices are correct:

content.text: Anyone is capable of improving themselves if they have the motivation to act.

explanationText.text: Charles Finney says that "Christian perfection is attainable in this life." So, Finney would likely agree that it is always possible to improve yourself and strive toward perfection.

content.text: Just as God is kind to others, you should care about the well-being of those around you.

explanationText.text: Charles Finney says that people should "seek the good of others with as single an eye as [God] does." Single means focused. So, Finney would likely agree that you should care about the well-being of those around you, just as God is kind to others.

contents.text: These choices are not correct:

content.text: You should prioritize helping those who are already good people to avoid sinful influences.

explanationText.text: Charles Finney says God cares about the happiness of everyone, from "the highest angel to the smallest worm." So, Finney would likely disagree that you should only help those who are already good people.

content.text: Only God has the power for perfection, so you should be content with what you have.

explanationText.text: Charles Finney says that Christian perfection is attainable if you "use…the powers you possess." So, Finney would likely disagree that only God has the power for perfection.

. Equiano wrote that he was born free in Africa but was captured and enslaved as a child. In the following excerpt, he describes his experiences on a slave ship bound for the Americas. Read the excerpt. Then answer the question below.

contents.text: Abolitionist societies committed to ending slavery began forming around the time of the American Revolution. They were often motivated by the ideals of liberty, human rights, and moral responsibility. Read the information about attempts to end slavery in the early United States. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: 1775: The Pennsylvania Abolition Society, one of the first U.S. antislavery organizations, is founded by doctor and politician Benjamin Rush.
1780: Pennsylvania passes the first gradual emancipation law, which frees children of enslaved people when they reach age 28 but does not free currently enslaved people.
1784: Benjamin Rush publishes a pamphlet arguing that slavery is a moral evil that threatens the ideals of liberty.
1787: Congress passes the Northwest Ordinance, prohibiting slavery in the future states of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, and Wisconsin. It is one of the first government restrictions of slavery.
1790: Benjamin Franklin petitions Congress to end the slave trade and to promote gradual emancipation of enslaved people.
1808: Congress ends the international slave trade, but the domestic slave trade remains legal in many states.

contents.text: Which of the following statements are supported by the events above? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Early abolitionists formed societies, wrote pamphlets, and drafted petitions to further their cause.
Early abolitionist efforts focused on gradual change rather than immediately banning slavery nationwide.
In the late 1700s, Congress limited the growth of slavery in some territories that would later become states.
Organized movements to end the slave trade and free enslaved persons did not begin until the early 1800s.

spread through much of the United States. Many preachers spoke about slavery during their sermons. Read the following excerpts from two Second Great Awakening preachers. Then answer the question below.

As soon as light prevails on this subject, men can no longer go on in the same course of sustaining the system, without the greatest guilt.…We, Christian men of the North, are all agreed that slavery is a great sin.…The public mind will and must act on [the question of slavery], and the action taken is continually affecting the honor of Christianity and the welfare of the church…

The case of Human Rights against Slavery has been [decided] in the court of conscience [many times]. The same verdict has always been rendered—"Guilty;" the same sentence has always been pronounced, "Let it be [condemned]"…

Early abolitionists often focused on the slave trade conditions. One of the most vivid descriptions of life aboard a slave ship comes from a book written by

. Equiano wrote that he was born free in Africa but was captured and enslaved as a child. In the following excerpt, he describes his experiences on a slave ship bound for the Americas. Read the excerpt. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: I was soon put down under the decks, and there I received such a salutation in my nostrils as I had never experienced in my life.…I became so sick and so low that I was not able to eat.…But soon, to my grief, two of the white men offered me [food]; and, on my refusing to eat, one of them held me fast by the hand…and tied my feet, while the other flogged me severely.…I would have jumped over the side, but I could not; and, besides, the crew used to watch us very closely…lest we should leap into the water.

the personal freedoms granted to enslaved people

contents.text: Abolitionist societies committed to ending slavery began forming around the time of the American Revolution. They were often motivated by the ideals of liberty, human rights, and moral responsibility. Read the information about attempts to end slavery in the early United States. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: 1775: The Pennsylvania Abolition Society, one of the first U.S. antislavery organizations, is founded by doctor and politician Benjamin Rush.
1780: Pennsylvania passes the first gradual emancipation law, which frees children of enslaved people when they reach age 28 but does not free currently enslaved people.
1784: Benjamin Rush publishes a pamphlet arguing that slavery is a moral evil that threatens the ideals of liberty.
1787: Congress passes the Northwest Ordinance, prohibiting slavery in the future states of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, and Wisconsin. It is one of the first government restrictions of slavery.
1790: Benjamin Franklin petitions Congress to end the slave trade and to promote gradual emancipation of enslaved people.
1808: Congress ends the international slave trade, but the domestic slave trade remains legal in many states.

pieces.text: In the early 1800s, a Christian religious movement called the

spread through much of the United States. Many preachers spoke about slavery during their sermons. Read the following excerpts from two Second Great Awakening preachers. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: The question now has taken this form; shall we individually and personally aid in making men slaves?…[Slavery]. As soon as light prevails on this subject, men can no longer go on in the same course of sustaining the system, without the greatest guilt.…We, Christian men of the North, are all agreed that slavery is a great sin.…The public mind will and must act on [the question of slavery], and the action taken is continually affecting the honor of Christianity and the welfare of the church…

meaning.text: immoral action or violation of God's law

textContent.text: You have common sense, and conscience, and a human heart;—pronounce upon it. You have a wife, or a husband, a child, a father, a mother, a brother or a sister—make the case your own, make it theirs, and bring in your verdict. The case of Human Rights against Slavery has been [decided] in the court of conscience [many times]. The same verdict has always been rendered—"Guilty;" the same sentence has always been pronounced, "Let it be [condemned]"…

choices.text: The church could meet its moral obligation by ensuring slavery didn't reach the North.
Everyone had an obligation to also convince other people that slavery should be illegal.
Even though slavery was wrong, Christians were called to uphold it because it was legal.
The institution of slavery was immoral because it violated God's law and human rights.

contents.text: Abolitionist societies committed to ending slavery began forming around the time of the American Revolution. They were often motivated by the ideals of liberty, human rights, and moral responsibility. Read the information about attempts to end slavery in the early United States. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: 1775: The Pennsylvania Abolition Society, one of the first U.S. antislavery organizations, is founded by doctor and politician Benjamin Rush.
1780: Pennsylvania passes the first gradual emancipation law, which frees children of enslaved people when they reach age 28 but does not free currently enslaved people.
1784: Benjamin Rush publishes a pamphlet arguing that slavery is a moral evil that threatens the ideals of liberty.
1787: Congress passes the Northwest Ordinance, prohibiting slavery in the future states of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, and Wisconsin. It is one of the first government restrictions of slavery.
1790: Benjamin Franklin petitions Congress to end the slave trade and to promote gradual emancipation of enslaved people.
1808: Congress ends the international slave trade, but the domestic slave trade remains legal in many states.

spread through much of the United States. Many preachers spoke about slavery during their sermons. Read the following excerpts from two Second Great Awakening preachers. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: The question now has taken this form; shall we individually and personally aid in making men slaves?…[Slavery]. As soon as light prevails on this subject, men can no longer go on in the same course of sustaining the system, without the greatest guilt.…We, Christian men of the North, are all agreed that slavery is a great sin.…The public mind will and must act on [the question of slavery], and the action taken is continually affecting the honor of Christianity and the welfare of the church…

meaning.text: immoral action or violation of God's law

textContent.text: You have common sense, and conscience, and a human heart;—pronounce upon it. You have a wife, or a husband, a child, a father, a mother, a brother or a sister—make the case your own, make it theirs, and bring in your verdict. The case of Human Rights against Slavery has been [decided] in the court of conscience [many times]. The same verdict has always been rendered—"Guilty;" the same sentence has always been pronounced, "Let it be [condemned]"…

textContent.text: I was soon put down under the decks, and there I received such a salutation in my nostrils as I had never experienced in my life.…I became so sick and so low that I was not able to eat.…But soon, to my grief, two of the white men offered me [food]; and, on my refusing to eat, one of them held me fast by the hand…and tied my feet, while the other flogged me severely.…I would have jumped over the side, but I could not; and, besides, the crew used to watch us very closely…lest we should leap into the water.

contents.text: What conditions did Equiano experience during the Transatlantic Slave Trade?

choices.text: Even though life was difficult on the slave ships, he was allowed some personal freedoms.
He was exposed to unsanitary conditions, terrible smells, illness, and abuse by the crew.
He was able to escape by jumping overboard and swimming away, since he was not closely guarded.
His living quarters were uncomfortable, but he received adequate food and medical attention.

contents.text: Look back at the excerpt. This choice is correct:

content.text: He was exposed to unsanitary conditions, terrible smells, illness, and abuse by the crew.

explanationText.text: Equiano describes very bad smells, illness, and beatings he endured on the slave ships.

contents.text: These choices are not correct:

content.text: Even though life was difficult on the slave ships, he was allowed some personal freedoms.

explanationText.text: Life was difficult on slave ships, but the passage does not mention any personal freedoms.

content.text: He was able to escape by jumping overboard and swimming away, since he was not closely guarded.

explanationText.text: Equiano was watched closely so he would not jump overboard or swim away.

content.text: His living quarters were uncomfortable, but he received adequate food and medical attention.

explanationText.text: Equiano describes being so sick he was unable to eat and being beaten and flogged instead of receiving medical attention.

contents.text: Abolitionist societies committed to ending slavery began forming around the time of the American Revolution. They were often motivated by the ideals of liberty, human rights, and moral responsibility. Read the information about attempts to end slavery in the early United States. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: 1775: The Pennsylvania Abolition Society, one of the first U.S. antislavery organizations, is founded by doctor and politician Benjamin Rush.
1780: Pennsylvania passes the first gradual emancipation law, which frees children of enslaved people when they reach age 28 but does not free currently enslaved people.
1784: Benjamin Rush publishes a pamphlet arguing that slavery is a moral evil that threatens the ideals of liberty.
1787: Congress passes the Northwest Ordinance, prohibiting slavery in the future states of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, and Wisconsin. It is one of the first government restrictions of slavery.
1790: Benjamin Franklin petitions Congress to end the slave trade and to promote gradual emancipation of enslaved people.
1808: Congress ends the international slave trade, but the domestic slave trade remains legal in many states.

spread through much of the United States. Many preachers spoke about slavery during their sermons. Read the following excerpts from two Second Great Awakening preachers. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: The question now has taken this form; shall we individually and personally aid in making men slaves?…[Slavery]. As soon as light prevails on this subject, men can no longer go on in the same course of sustaining the system, without the greatest guilt.…We, Christian men of the North, are all agreed that slavery is a great sin.…The public mind will and must act on [the question of slavery], and the action taken is continually affecting the honor of Christianity and the welfare of the church…

lessons.name: Source analysis: What to the slave is the Fourth of July?

contents.text: The speech "What to the slave is the Fourth of July?" was delivered by Frederick Douglass on July 5, 1852, in Rochester, New York. In the mid-nineteenth century, Fourth of July orations were typically celebratory speeches that glorified the American Revolution and praised the ideals of liberty and independence. In a period of growing tensions over slavery, Douglass used the occasion to highlight the contradiction of celebrating freedom in a country that enslaved millions of African American people.

When historians study a text, they consider how events in the author's life may have shaped the author's point of view. Match each piece of context from Douglass's background to the corresponding detail about Douglass's speech.

draggableItems.text: Douglass provided a firsthand account of the brutality of slavery.
Douglass was invited to speak because he was a famous writer and orator.
Douglass wanted to disprove ideas about the intellectual inferiority of African American individuals.
Douglass wanted to use his speech to increase support for the antislavery movement.

staticItems.text: Douglass was born into slavery in 1818. He was separated from his family at age 6, when he was sent to work on Wye House Plantation.
Enslaved people were not taught to read and write, although Douglass secretly taught himself.
After escaping from slavery in 1838, Douglass moved to Massachusetts and became a leader in the abolition movement.
Douglass published his first autobiography in 1845, which soon became a bestseller. He traveled throughout the U.S. and to Britain and Ireland to give speeches.

pieces.text: Friends and Fellow Citizens: He who could address this audience without a
sensation has stronger nerves than I have. I do not remember ever to have appeared as a speaker before any assembly more

, nor with greater distrust of my ability than I do this day. A feeling has crept over me, quite unfavorable to the exercise of my limited powers of speech.…The little experience I have in addressing public meetings in country schoolhouses, avails me nothing to the present occasion.

The papers and placards say that I am to deliver a Fourth of July oration. This certainly sounds large…[and] it is true that I have often had the privilege to speak in this beautiful Hall, and to address many who now honor me with their presence. But neither the familiar faces, nor the perfect
I think I have of [the venue], seems to free me from embarrassment.

I think I have of [the venue], seems to free me from embarrassment.

textContent.text: The fact is, ladies and gentlemen, the distance between this platform and the slave plantation, from which I escaped, is considerable.…That I am here today is, to me, a matter of astonishment as well as of gratitude.…With little experience and with less learning, I have been able to throw my thoughts hastily and imperfectly together; and trusting to your patient and generous [kindness] I will proceed to lay them before you.

contents.text: The speech "What to the slave is the Fourth of July?" was delivered by Frederick Douglass on July 5, 1852, in Rochester, New York. In the mid-nineteenth century, Fourth of July orations were typically celebratory speeches that glorified the American Revolution and praised the ideals of liberty and independence. In a period of growing tensions over slavery, Douglass used the occasion to highlight the contradiction of celebrating freedom in a country that enslaved millions of African American people.
